claim: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is characterized by the progressive degeneration of motoneurons in the primary motor cortex (pMO) and in spinal cord.
source: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is characterized by the progressive degeneration of motoneurons in the primary motor cortex (pMO) and in spinal cord.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract describing the classical characterization of ALS, supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Functional MRI studies demonstrate an increase in functional connectivity in areas connected to pMO despite the ongoing neurodegeneration in ALS.
source: However, the pathogenic process involves multiple subnetworks in the brain and functional MRI studies demonstrate an increase in functional connectivity in areas connected to pMO despite the ongoing neurodegeneration.
evidence: This claim references functional MRI studies that have been conducted, implying citation to existing literature.

claim: A new retrograde AAV9 variant was developed to quantitatively map projections to pMO in the SOD1(G93A) ALS mouse model.
source: We have developed a new retrograde AAV9 to quantitatively map the projections to pMO in the SOD1(G93A) ALS mouse model.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study describing the development and application of a new viral tool.

claim: There is an increase in the number of neurons projecting from somatosensory cortex to pMO at presymptomatic stages in the SOD1(G93A) ALS mouse model.
source: We show an increase in the number of neurons projecting from somatosensory cortex to pMO at presymptomatic stages, followed by an increase in projections from thalamus, auditory cortex and contralateral MO (inputs from 20 other structures remains unchanged) as disease advances.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study based on viral tracing data.

claim: Projections from thalamus, auditory cortex and contralateral MO to pMO increase as disease advances in the SOD1(G93A) ALS mouse model.
source: We show an increase in the number of neurons projecting from somatosensory cortex to pMO at presymptomatic stages, followed by an increase in projections from thalamus, auditory cortex and contralateral MO (inputs from 20 other structures remains unchanged) as disease advances.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study based on viral tracing data at different disease stages.

claim: Inputs from 20 other structures to pMO remain unchanged during disease progression in the SOD1(G93A) ALS mouse model.
source: We show an increase in the number of neurons projecting from somatosensory cortex to pMO at presymptomatic stages, followed by an increase in projections from thalamus, auditory cortex and contralateral MO (inputs from 20 other structures remains unchanged) as disease advances.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study based on viral tracing data.

claim: Pathological hallmarks of ALS (such as TDP-43 inclusions) appear in motor cortex as well as in multiple cortical and subcortical structures during disease progression.
source: However, postmortem studies have demonstrated that pathological hallmarks of ALS (such as TDP-43 inclusions) appear in motor cortex as well as in multiple cortical and subcortical structures during disease progression, depicting a propagation pattern (Brettschneider et al., 2013; Braak et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to postmortem studies by Brettschneider et al., 2013 and Braak et al., 2013.

claim: ALS has been growingly conceptualized as a disease of the motor subnetwork or, in more advanced stages, a multi-network disease affecting motor, premotor and sensory areas.
source: Thus, ALS has been growingly conceptualized as a disease of the motor subnetwork or, in more advanced stages, a multi-network disease affecting motor, premotor and sensory areas.
evidence: This reflects a conceptual shift in the field based on accumulated evidence, representing established knowledge.

claim: DTI studies have revealed that the degeneration of axons is detected in more and more white-matter tracts affecting different structures at different stages of the propagation scheme in ALS.
source: Diffusion-tensor imaging (DTI) studies have revealed that the degeneration of axons is detected in more and more white-matter tracts affecting different structures (corticospinal, corticorubral, corticostriatal and perforant tracts) at different stages of the propagation scheme (Neuroimaging Society in ALS (NiSALS) DTI Study Group et al., 2016; Kassubek et al., 2014; Kassubek et al., 2018) as well as in interhemispheric connections (Filippini et al., 2010) and in spinal cord (Cohen-Adad et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to DTI studies.

claim: Increased functional connectivity has been described in symptomatic ALS patients in the sensorimotor, somatosensory and cortico-striatal networks.
source: However, analysis of resting-state networks by functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) has revealed increased functional connectivity has been described in symptomatic ALS patients in the sensorimotor (Menke et al., 2016; Agosta et al., 2018) somatosensory (Agosta et al., 2011) and cortico-striatal networks (Fekete et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple fMRI studies.

claim: An increase in functional connectivity in the motor subnetwork was already detectable in presymptomatic and early-stage ALS patients.
source: Notably, an increase in functional connectivity in the motor subnetwork was already detectable in presymptomatic and early-stage ALS patients (Schulthess et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Schulthess et al., 2016.

claim: AAV9-SLR displayed a significantly higher local infection rate than WT-AAV9 (143 ± 10%; post-hoc p=0.0001).
source: Compared to WT-AAV9, infection rate was significantly higher for AAV9-SLR (post-hoc p=0.0001) but not for AAV-NSS, (p=0.0910), and was significantly lower for both AAV-RGD (p=0.0001) and WT-AAV2 (p=0.0001; detailed statistics are reported in Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study comparing viral variants, with data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: AAV9-SLR produced a ten-fold increase in retrogradely infected TH+ neurons compared to WT-AAV9 (1267 ± 152%, p=0.0001) after dorsal striatum injection.
source: after DS injection, rAAV9-SLR produced a ten-fold increase in retrogradely infected TH +neurons compared to WT-AAV9 (1267 ± 152%, p=0.0001); rAAV9-NSS was more effective than WT-AAV9 (600 ± 100%, p=0.0001) but less effective than AAV9-SLR.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study, with data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: AAV9-SLR displayed the highest rate of retrograde infection in motor cortex (236 ± 32% of WT-AAV9, p=0.0001) after dorsal striatum injection.
source: after DS injection, rAAV9-SLR displayed the highest rate of retrograde infection in motor cortex (236 ± 32% of WT-AAV9, p=0.0001), followed by rAAV9-NSS (145 ± 25% p=0.0909), both more effective than WT-AAV9.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study, with data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: AAV9-SLR displayed a strong retrograde infection of LGN neurons (700 ± 240%, p=0.0005) after injection in primary visual cortex.
source: rAAV9-SLR displayed a strong retrograde infection of LGN neurons (700 ± 240%, p=0.0005), followed by AAV9-NSS (400 ± 133% of WT-AAV9, p=0.0446).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study, with data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: 28 distinct anatomical structures provide direct input to the injection site in pMO in wild-type mice.
source: Overall, we identified 28 distinct anatomical structures providing direct input to the injection site in pMO, including thalamic nuclei (TH; Figure 2D), followed by homolateral somatosensory cortex (SS; Figure 2D), contralateral secondary motor cortex (cMOs) and contralateral primary motor cortex (cMOp; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study mapping inputs to pMO, with data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Thalamus represents 32 ± 7% of the total input to pMO in wild-type mice.
source: When projecting neurons are expressed in terms of percentage of the total population of projecting neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), TH represented 32 ± 7% of the total input to pMO, SS 22 ± 7%, cMOs 8 ± 3% and cMOp 6 ± 2% (full details are provided for all structures in Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study quantifying inputs to pMO.

claim: Somatosensory cortex represents 22 ± 7% of the total input to pMO in wild-type mice.
source: When projecting neurons are expressed in terms of percentage of the total population of projecting neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), TH represented 32 ± 7% of the total input to pMO, SS 22 ± 7%, cMOs 8 ± 3% and cMOp 6 ± 2% (full details are provided for all structures in Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study quantifying inputs to pMO.

claim: A subset of neurons projecting to pMO is located in hypothalamus (0.6 ± 0.2% of the total pool of neurons projecting to pMO in the forebrain).
source: We consistently identified a small contingent of neurons projecting to pMO located in hypothalamus (HY 0.6 ± 0.2% of the total pool of neurons projecting to pMO in the forebrain); out of these hypothalamic neurons, not previously reported, the majority was located in the lateral zone of hypothalamus (zona incerta 23 ± 10% of the total of hypothalamic neurons projecting to pMO; lateral preoptic area 23 ± 19% of the total of hypothalamic neurons projecting to pMO; lateral hypothalamic area 14 ± 18% of the total of hypothalamic neurons projecting to pMO).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study identifying a previously unreported input to pMO.

claim: Additional inputs to pMO were identified from paraventricular hypothalamic area (PAL 0.8 ± 0.2) and gustatory area (GU 0.7 ± 0.3).
source: In addition to previously reported input structures to pMO (Hooks et al., 2013; Oh et al., 2014; Mao et al., 2011), we identified additional inputs from paraventricular hypothalamic area (PAL 0.8 ± 0.2) and gustatory area (GU 0.7 ± 0.3%).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study identifying previously unreported inputs to pMO, with reference to prior literature.

claim: Input toward pMO and sMO is qualitatively similar.
source: The input to the neighboring sMO was qualitatively similar to pMO, including all of the structures projecting to pMO (all in all, 20 distinct regions were found to project to sMO compared to 28 for pMO).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study comparing inputs to pMO and sMO.

claim: Somatosensory cortex contributes a significantly larger share of input to sMO than to pMO (33 ± 3%, p<0.0001 vs pMO).
source: When projecting neurons are expressed in terms of percentage of the total population of projecting neurons (Supplementary file 1, Figure 2D), SS emerged as contributing a significantly larger share of input to sMO than to pMO (33 ± 3%, p<0.0001 vs pMO), followed by structures whose input to pMO and sMO was comparable (detailed values reported in Supplementary file 1g): TH (28 ± 1%, p=0.5965), AUD (10 ± 2%, p=0.1914), cMOs (7 ± 3%, p>0.9999), cMOp (4 ± 1%, p=0.9815), orbital area (ORB: 2 ± 0.4%, p>0.9999) and BLA (2 ± 0.7%, p>0.9999).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study comparing inputs to pMO and sMO.

claim: 19 thalamic nuclei were found to project to either pMO or sMO motor cortex.
source: In total, 19 thalamic nuclei were found to project to either pMO or sMO motor cortex (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–F).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study mapping thalamic inputs to motor cortex.

claim: The ventral anterior-lateral complex and the ventral medial nucleus are the most relevant source of projection to MO from thalamus.
source: When considered as a fraction of the total number of thalamic neurons projecting to pMO or sMO, the ventral anterior-lateral complex and the ventral medial nucleus appeared to be the most relevant source of projection to MO, and their contribution to pMO or sMO was comparable (VAL to pMO 29 ± 6%, to sMO 34 ± 6%, two-way ANOVA p=0.6496) and ventral medial nucleus (VM to pMO 24 ± 7%, to sMO 25 ± 12%, p>0.9999; detailed values reported in Supplementary file 1j).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study analyzing thalamic inputs to motor cortex.

claim: There is an overall increase in the number of neurons projecting to pMO in mSOD compared to WT at P35 (early-presymptomatic stage).
source: Strikingly, we found an overall increase in the number of neurons projecting to pMO in mSOD compared to WT both in raw counts (Supplementary file 2a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and after normalization (Two-way ANOVA, brain regions F(26,189)=53.0 p<0.0001, genotype F(1,189)=16.3 p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study comparing mSOD and WT mice at early presymptomatic stage.

claim: At P35, mSOD mice display a statistically significant increase in the mean number of neurons projecting to pMO from SS (effect size: 1.6; p<0.0001).
source: Post-hoc analysis (Figure 3B; detailed numerical values in Supplementary file 2b) revealed a statistically significant increase in the mean number of neurons projecting to pMO from SS (effect size: 1.6; p<0.0001) and from cMOs (effect size: 1.6; p=0.0189).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study comparing mSOD and WT mice at early presymptomatic stage.

claim: At P35, mSOD mice display a statistically significant increase in the mean number of neurons projecting to pMO from cMOs (effect size: 1.6; p=0.0189).
source: Post-hoc analysis (Figure 3B; detailed numerical values in Supplementary file 2b) revealed a statistically significant increase in the mean number of neurons projecting to pMO from SS (effect size: 1.6; p<0.0001) and from cMOs (effect size: 1.6; p=0.0189).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study comparing mSOD and WT mice at early presymptomatic stage.

claim: Despite the overall increase in projection from SS to pMO in mSOD mice at P35, a significant loss of projections from layer V of SS was detected (WT 46 ± 9% vs mSOD 30 ± 2%, p=0.0324).
source: Interestingly, despite the overall increase in the number of neurons projecting to pMO, a significant loss of projecting neurons was detected in SS layer V of mSOD mice (effect size: −1.5; p=0.0324, Supplementary file 2a) mirrored by a reciprocal trend toward increase projection from layer II/III (effect size: 1.2; p=0.2734) but not in layer VI (p=0.9898).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study analyzing layer-specific changes in projections.

claim: CTb labeled a larger number of neurons in the SS in the mSOD compared to WT at P35 (SS effect size: 1.4; p=0.0156).
source: Confirming the viral tracing data, CTb labeled a larger number of neurons in the SS in the mSOD compared to WT (both N = 3; one-way ANOVA F(3,8)=17.0, p=0.0008), whereas no difference was detected in cMOp between the two genotypes (SS effect size: 1.4; p=0.0156, cMOp effect size: −0.4; p=0.9971; Figure 4A–C and Supplementary file 2g).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study using an independent tracing method to confirm viral tracing results.

claim: No difference was detected in cMOp between mSOD and WT genotypes at P35 using CTb tracing (cMOp effect size: −0.4; p=0.9971).
source: Confirming the viral tracing data, CTb labeled a larger number of neurons in the SS in the mSOD compared to WT (both N = 3; one-way ANOVA F(3,8)=17.0, p=0.0008), whereas no difference was detected in cMOp between the two genotypes (SS effect size: 1.4; p=0.0156, cMOp effect size: −0.4; p=0.9971; Figure 4A–C and Supplementary file 2g).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study using CTb tracing to validate viral tracing results.

claim: No difference in projections from LGN and MO to V1 was found between WT and mSOD at P35.
source: Injection of AAV9-SLR in V1 resulted in a comparable number of labelled neurons (either before either after normalization for the injection site volume: Supplementary file 2h and 2i) in WT (N = 3) and mSOD (N = 3) both in LGN (p=0.9263) and in MO (p=0.6360).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study demonstrating specificity of changes to motor network.

claim: Input to sMO was comparable in WT and mSOD mice at P35.
source: In contrast to our observation in the pMO, input to sMO was comparable in WT (N = 3) and mSOD (N = 4) mice (either before either after normalization; for normalized two- way ANOVA, genotype F(1,100)=0.7572 p=0.3863. Figure 5A–C and Supplementary file 2j and 2k for non-normalized and normalized counts, respectively).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study comparing inputs to sMO in WT and mSOD mice.

claim: At P60, mSOD mice displayed an increase in neurons projecting to pMO from SS (effect size: 1.6; p=0.0019).
source: However, when compared to their age-matched WT littermates at P60, mSOD mice displayed an increase in neurons projecting to pMO (two-way ANOVA; brain regions F(19,100)=2.3 p=0.0034) from SS (effect size: 1.6; p=0.0019; unchanged compared to P20 mSOD, p>0.9999) and cMOs (effect size: 1.6; p=0.0454; unchanged compared to P20 mSOD, p>0.9999).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study tracking disease progression.

claim: At P60, mSOD mice displayed an increase in neurons projecting to pMO from cMOs (effect size: 1.6; p=0.0454).
source: However, when compared to their age-matched WT littermates at P60, mSOD mice displayed an increase in neurons projecting to pMO (two-way ANOVA; brain regions F(19,100)=2.3 p=0.0034) from SS (effect size: 1.6; p=0.0019; unchanged compared to P20 mSOD, p>0.9999) and cMOs (effect size: 1.6; p=0.0454; unchanged compared to P20 mSOD, p>0.9999).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study tracking disease progression.

claim: At P60, an increased number of neurons projecting to pMO was found in cMOp (effect size: 1.4; p=0.0077 in mSOD vs WT littermates).
source: In addition, now an increased number of neurons projecting to pMO was found in cMOp (effect size: 1.4; p=0.0077 in mSOD vs WT littermates,+2.4 ± 0.9 vs P20 mSOD, p=0.0110).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study tracking disease progression.

claim: At P90, projections to pMO from SS were still increased in mSOD mice (effect size:1.6; p=0.0095).
source: Projections to pMO from SS was still increased (effect size:1.6; p=0.0095; same increase registered for P20 and P60 mSOD, p>0.9999 for both), cMOp (effect size: 1.7; p<0.0001, also increased when compared to the P60 timepoint:+1.6 ± 0.5 vs P60 mSOD, p=0.0124) and cMOs (Effect size: 1.4; p<0.0001, comparable to the increase registered in mSOD at P20 (p=0.7658) and P60 (p=0.3917)).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study tracking disease progression to symptomatic stage.

claim: At P90, increased number of projecting neurons was detected from TH (effect size: 1.7; p=0.0014) in mSOD mice.
source: Moreover, increased number of projecting neurons was detected from TH (effect size: 1.7; p=0.0014;+1.8 ± 0.4 vs P20 mSOD, p=0.0064), AUD (effect size: 1.6; p<0.0001;+1.4 ± 0.5 vs P20 mSOD, p<0.0001), and CP (effect size: 1.7; p<0.0001;+2.0 ± 0.5 vs P20 mSOD, p=0.0086).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study tracking disease progression to symptomatic stage.

claim: At P90, increased number of projecting neurons was detected from AUD (effect size: 1.6; p<0.0001) in mSOD mice.
source: Moreover, increased number of projecting neurons was detected from TH (effect size: 1.7; p=0.0014;+1.8 ± 0.4 vs P20 mSOD, p=0.0064), AUD (effect size: 1.6; p<0.0001;+1.4 ± 0.5 vs P20 mSOD, p<0.0001), and CP (effect size: 1.7; p<0.0001;+2.0 ± 0.5 vs P20 mSOD, p=0.0086).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study tracking disease progression to symptomatic stage.

claim: At P90, increased number of projecting neurons was detected from CP (effect size: 1.7; p<0.0001) in mSOD mice.
source: Moreover, increased number of projecting neurons was detected from TH (effect size: 1.7; p=0.0014;+1.8 ± 0.4 vs P20 mSOD, p=0.0064), AUD (effect size: 1.6; p<0.0001;+1.4 ± 0.5 vs P20 mSOD, p<0.0001), and CP (effect size: 1.7; p<0.0001;+2.0 ± 0.5 vs P20 mSOD, p=0.0086).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study tracking disease progression to symptomatic stage.

claim: No difference in the total number of neurons in pMO was detected between WT and mSOD at P90 (WT: 1087 ± 128 vs mSOD 1087 ± 236).
source: To exclude an effect of a widespread neuronal loss in the pMO of mSOD on the number of axons projecting to pMO, we performed a NeuN staining in the pMO of P90 mSOD mice (n = 3) revealing no difference in the total number of neurons in our injection area (p=0.4987, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study ruling out neuronal loss as a confounding factor.

claim: At P60, layer-V neurons projecting to pMO in SS, AUD and cMO displayed a decrease in spine density in mSOD mice.
source: Interestingly, layer-V neurons projecting to the pMO in SS, AUD and cMO displayed a decrease in spine density from P60 (Figure 7B), (F(13,119)=7.8, p<0.0001); at the same time- point, a decrease in dendritic spine density in neurons from layer V of pMO itself became evident (p=0.0071; in agreement with what previously reported; Ozdinler et al., 2011; detailed numerical values are reported in Supplementary file 3c).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study analyzing dendritic spine pathology.

claim: At P60, no statistically significant change in spine density was found in layer II/III in any of the cortical areas considered.
source: Unlike layer V, we found no statistically significant change in the spine density in layer II/III at P60 in any of the cortical areas considered.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study analyzing dendritic spine pathology.

claim: At P90, a significant decrease in spine density affected neurons projecting to pMO from all structures under scrutiny either in layer II/III or in layer V (effect size between −1.6 and −1.8; F(13,128)=47.8, p<0.0001).
source: At P90, a significant decrease in spine density affected neurons projecting to pMO from all structures under scrutiny either in layer II/III either in layer V (effect size between −1.6 and −1.8; F(13,128)=47.8, p<0.0001, Figure 7C and Supplementary file 3d).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study analyzing dendritic spine pathology at symptomatic stage.

claim: At P35, 41 ± 7% of neurons in pMO layer V were positive for misfSOD compared to only 1 ± 0.5% of layer II/III neurons.
source: In pMO, where upper MN are mainly (but not exclusively) localized, already at this age 41 ± 7% of neurons in pMO layer V were positive for misfSOD +compared to only 1 ± 0.5% of layer II/III neurons.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study analyzing misfolded SOD1 distribution.

claim: Both SS and AUD included a misfSOD+ subset of neurons in layer II/III (20 ± 5%) and layer V (54 ± 6%).
source: Both SS and AUD included a misfSOD +subset of neurons in layer II/III (20 ± 5%) and layer V (54 ± 6%).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study analyzing misfolded SOD1 distribution.

claim: In layers II/III and V, the population of neurons projecting to pMO (CTb+) displayed a significantly lower burden of misfSOD1 than the overall neuronal population of the CTb- neurons (effect size between −0.9 and −1.4; one-way ANOVA, F(11,1242) = 35.3, p<0.0001).
source: However, when we considered the CTb + and CTb- subpopulations of neurons, we found that, in layers II/III and V the population of neurons projecting to pMO (CTb+) displayed a significantly lower burden of misfSOD1 than the overall neuronal population of the CTb- neurons (effect size between −0.9 and −1.4; one-way ANOVA, F(11,1242) = 35.3, p<0.0001; Figure 8A–C and detailed numerical values in Supplementary file 3e) in both cortical layers of SS (p<0.0001) as well as in both cortical layers of AUD (p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study analyzing misfolded SOD1 in projection neurons.

claim: SS subpopulation projecting to contralateral SS displayed a range of misfSOD levels comparable to non-projecting, nearby neurons (p=0.2696).
source: In contrast to what observed in the subpopulation connected to pMO, SS subpopulation projecting to contralateral SS displayed a range of misfSOD levels comparable to non-projecting, nearby neurons (p=0.2696) including, in both cases, neurons with high burden and neurons with low burden of mSOD (Figure 8D–E and Supplementary file 3f).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study demonstrating specificity of misfSOD distribution in pMO-projecting neurons.

claim: Despite the extreme difference in misfSOD burden, spine density was comparable in high and low misfSOD expression groups at P60.
source: Interestingly, despite the extreme difference in misfSOD burden, spine density was comparable in two groups and was within the range of WT mice for layer II/III neurons and reduced (compared to WT) for layer V neurons (in agreement with the values in Figure 7B; statistic in Supplementary file 3g), suggesting that spine loss may be a non-cell-autonomous phenomenon not directly related to the burden of mistSOD.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study analyzing the relationship between misfSOD and spine pathology.

claim: Network-based statistics of functional connectome data revealed significantly increased functional connectivity (hyper-connectivity) between regions frontal to the pMO, namely the dorsolateral prefrontal association cortex and the pMO itself, both homolaterally and contralaterally (t ≥ 2.81, p≤0.0065, corrected) in ALS patients.
source: However, network-based statistics of functional connectome data revealed significantly increased functional connectivity (hyper-connectivity) between regions frontal to the pMO, namely the dorsolateral prefrontal association cortex and the pMO itself, both homolaterally and contralaterally (t ≥ 2.81, p≤0.0065, corrected; Figure 9B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the human fMRI study.

claim: Functional connectivity between left and right primary somatosensory cortex was decreased in ALS patients (t = 2.93, p=0.0048).
source: Functional connectivity between left and right primary somatosensory cortex was decreased (t = 2.93, p=0.0048) and no effect was detected between thalamic nuclei and pMO or in visual cortex.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the human fMRI study.

claim: No effect was detected between thalamic nuclei and pMO or in visual cortex in ALS patients.
source: Functional connectivity between left and right primary somatosensory cortex was decreased (t = 2.93, p=0.0048) and no effect was detected between thalamic nuclei and pMO or in visual cortex.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the human fMRI study.

claim: The fMRI data from ALS patients confirmed the occurrence of a large-scale remodeling in the motor subnetwork.
source: Thus, the fMRI data from ALS patients confirmed the occurrence of a large-scale remodeling in the motor subnetwork (as observed in the murine dataset and confirming previously published data; Schulthess et al., 2016) and showed a predominant increase in connectivity between pMO and both homolateral and contralateral frontal-lobe areas, showing similarity with the increase projection from contralateral rostral structures, such as sMO, observed in the mouse model.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fMRI data in the context of the mouse model findings and prior literature.

claim: The pattern observed in the mouse model bears significant similarities with fMRI functional connectivity data gathered from human ALS patients.
source: We show that the pattern observed in the mouse model bears significant similarities with fMRI functional connectivity data gathered from human ALS patients.
evidence: This is a comparative conclusion drawn from both mouse and human data in the study.

claim: The increase in projection to pMO may be interpreted as due to the expansion of the axonal arborizations of these neurons in pMO as disease progresses.
source: The increase in the number of neurons projecting to a fixed, small volume of pMO is most likely to be interpreted as due to the expansion of the axonal arborizations of these neurons in pMO as disease progresses and it is in agreement with the increased frequency of EPSPs observed early in disease course (Fogarty et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings with reference to prior literature.

claim: Silencing of either the pre- or post-synaptic site is sufficient to induce axonal sprouting in several models.
source: On the other hand, it has been demonstrated in several models (e.g. in the neuromuscular unit), that silencing of either the pre- or post-synaptic site is sufficient to induce axonal sprouting (Caroni et al., 1994; Caroni, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work by Caroni et al., 1994 and Caroni, 1997.

claim: Reduced firing of vulnerable spinal MN has been shown to precede degeneration.
source: Since reduced firing of vulnerable spinal MN has been shown to precede degeneration (Martínez-Silva et al., 2018; Roselli and Caroni, 2015), it is tempting to speculate that the expansion of the projections may be driven by abnormal activity of vulnerable post-synaptic neurons in the pMO (including vulnerable corticospinal MN; Ozdinler et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work by Martínez-Silva et al., 2018 and Roselli and Caroni, 2015.

claim: Structural connectivity is a strong predictor of functional connectivity at large-scale level.
source: Although the relationship between structural and functional connectivity is not precise, severals studies have demonstrated that, at large-scale level, structural connectivity is a strong predictor of functional connectivity (Honey et al., 2009; Honey et al., 2007; Damoiseaux and Greicius, 2009; Hermundstad et al., 2013) and maps of functional and structural connectivity display high degrees of similarity (van den Heuvel et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Anatomical connectivity strongly shapes functional connectivity in non-human primates.
source: Moreover, studies in non-human primates comparing functional connectivity with anatomical tracing have revealed that anatomical connectivity strongly (although not exclusively) shape the functional connectivity (Shen et al., 2012; Shen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work by Shen et al., 2012 and Shen et al., 2015.

claim: Calbindin-positive GABAergic interneurons undergo degeneration in ALS.
source: Changes in functional connectivity could also result from an alteration in the local excitation/inhibition balance due to the dysfunction of inhibitory interneurons (Douaud et al., 2011): in fact, pathological studies have found that calbindin-positive GABAergic interneurons undergo degeneration in ALS (Maekawa et al., 2004), lending support to the hypothesis that loss of inhibitory tone contributes to clinical dysfunction in ALS (Turner and Kiernan, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work by Maekawa et al., 2004.

claim: Spine loss has been detected as a morphological counterpart of the early stages of the degenerative process ongoing in the layer V of the motor cortex of mSOD mice.

claim: SS neurons appeared to be affected by spine loss only very late in disease progression (P120) in previous studies.

claim: AAV9-SLR is a new AAV variant endowed with robust, reproducible and broad retrograde infection capability.
source: Taken together, these data identified AAV9-SLR as a new AAV variant endowed with robust, reproducible and broad retrograde infection capability.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental characterization of the AAV9-SLR variant.

claim: AAV9 has reduced binding to heparin sulfate compared to AAV2.
source: Although rAAV2 belongs to the AAV2 serotype and may strongly bind heparan sulphate, our AAV9-derived retrograde AAV variant has the advantage of reduced binding to heparin sulfate (Shen et al., 2011) and therefore it is less affected by changes in brain extracellular matrix (e.g. due to neuroinflammation associated with neurodegeneration); AAV9 is only infrequently targeted by pre-existing immunity to AAVs (Zhang et al., 2011; Saraiva et al., 2016) and may provide the entry point to enhanced vectors for circuit-specific gene therapy in humans since AAV9 has been already successfully tested for this application (Boutin et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by Shen et al., 2011.

claim: The expansion of projections to pMO may contribute a structural substrate of the functional hyperconnectivity observed in fMRI studies.
source: Thus, on the assumption that the observations made on the remodelling of the motor subnetwork in mouse models could be extrapolated to humans, the expansion of projections to pMO may contribute a structural substrate of the functional hyperconnectivity observed in fMRI studies.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation linking mouse and human findings.

claim: The observed increase in projection from cortical and subcortical areas might be an early adaptive response to ongoing cell dysfunction.
source: The observed increase in projection from cortical and subcortical areas might be an early adaptive response to ongoing cell dysfunction up to the point where a critical cell loss is reached and a disconnection syndrome begins to emerge (Gorges et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings with reference to prior literature.
